Oil-sensitive stocks, including oil marketing companies (OMCs), paint manufacturers, tyre makers and aviation companies, rallied on Wednesday, November 11, as global crude oil prices eased to a two-month low, raising hopes of lower input costs and improved profitability.

Shares of companies such as HPCL, BPCL, Indian Oil Corporation (IOC), Asian Paints, Berger Paints and InterGlobe Aviation (IndiGo) are attracting investor attention as the decline in crude prices offers potential cost relief to several industries.
Lower crude prices can improve marketing margins for OMCs, ease raw material costs for paint and tyre manufacturers, and reduce fuel expenses for airlines.
The rally comes after Brent crude prices fell to their lowest level since August 31, amid easing concerns over further military escalation between the US and Iran. The global oil benchmark had settled at $91.49 per barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude closed at $86.04.
Here is how shares were faring
At 09:58 AM, HPCL shares traded nearly 3% higher at ₹397 apiece on the NSE, while Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) was up 0.65% at ₹147.80. Bharat Petroleum Corporation (BPCL) traded 1.36% higher at ₹320.30.
InterGlobe Aviation (IndiGo) was up 4.60% at ₹5,680 on the NSE; SpiceJet was up 0.36%.
Asian Paints shares were up around 2% to ₹2,557, while Berger Paints India was up 1.10% to ₹476.40 on the NSE. Kansai Nerolac Paints traded 0.2% higher at ₹201.38. Indigo Paints was up 2.6% at ₹938.85 on the NSE.
CEAT shares were up 1.72% at ₹3,515, while JK Tyre & Industries traded 0.36% higher at ₹358.60 on the NSE.
Reliance Industries shares traded 0.84% higher at ₹1,335.50 apiece on the NSE. Crude oil price movements can affect Reliance Industries' refining and petrochemical businesses by influencing feedstock costs, product prices and refining margins.
Lower crude prices can also lead to inventory losses, while higher prices may result in inventory gains, depending on the timing of price movements.
Details to know
Brent crude futures fell $1.08, or 1.2%, to settle at $91.49 per barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude declined 81 cents, or 0.9%, to $86.04 per barrel on Tuesday. Both benchmarks settled at their lowest levels since August 31 for a second consecutive session.
Crude oil prices fell by more than $3 per barrel in early trade on Tuesday before recovering some losses after Iran's top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, said there were currently no negotiations between Tehran and Washington.
The initial decline followed US Secretary of State Marco Rubio's comments to Group of Seven (G7) allies that economic sanctions and the naval blockade were working, reducing the need for major US combat operations against Iran.
The decline in crude oil prices matters for Indian companies, as the country relies heavily on imports to meet its crude oil needs.

Lower crude prices can ease input costs for several industries, although the impact varies depending on their exposure to oil, pricing power, inventory levels and currency movements.
OMCs: Lower crude prices could ease input costs
Oil marketing companies (OMCs), including Indian Oil Corporation (IOC), Bharat Petroleum Corporation (BPCL) and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation (HPCL), could benefit from a decline in crude oil prices as lower input costs can improve their marketing margins, provided retail fuel prices remain unchanged.
However, the extent of the benefit will depend on the companies' ability to pass on changes in crude prices to consumers, refining margins and inventory gains or losses.
If retail petrol and diesel prices are reduced in line with crude oil prices, the benefit to marketing margins could be limited.
ONGC, Oil India: Lower crude prices can weigh on upstream companies
In contrast, upstream oil producers such as Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) and Oil India could face pressure from declining crude oil prices.
These companies explore and produce crude oil and natural gas. Their realisations are linked to global crude oil prices. A sustained decline in crude prices could therefore reduce their revenue and operating profitability.
Higher crude prices generally benefit upstream producers by improving realisations, while a correction in prices can have the opposite impact.
Paint stocks: Lower raw material costs could support margins
Paint manufacturers such as Asian Paints, Berger Paints, Kansai Nerolac and Akzo Nobel India could benefit from lower crude oil prices.
Crude oil is an important raw material for the paint industry, as several inputs, including solvents, resins, monomers, and other petrochemical derivatives, are crude-linked.
A decline in crude prices can reduce procurement costs and support operating margins, particularly if companies do not immediately pass on the savings through lower product prices.
However, the impact may not be immediate as it depends on inventory costs, raw material procurement cycles and the movement of individual petrochemical prices.

Tyre stocks: Potential relief from crude-linked input costs
Tyre manufacturers, including MRF, Apollo Tyres, CEAT and JK Tyre, could also benefit from softer crude oil prices.
Synthetic rubber, carbon black and several chemicals used in tyre manufacturing are linked to crude oil and its derivatives. Lower crude prices can therefore ease raw material costs and support margins.
However, natural rubber is another major input for tyre manufacturers, and its prices are influenced by factors such as weather conditions, production and global supply-demand dynamics. Consequently, the benefits of lower crude prices may vary across companies.
Aviation stocks: Lower aviation turbine fuel costs could help airlines
Aviation companies such as InterGlobe Aviation (IndiGo) and SpiceJet could benefit from lower crude oil prices as aviation turbine fuel (ATF) accounts for a significant portion of their operating expenses.
ATF prices are linked to global petroleum product prices, which are influenced by crude oil movements. A sustained decline in crude prices could eventually translate into lower fuel expenses for airlines, supporting their operating margins.
However, the transmission is not instantaneous, and ATF prices in India are revised periodically. The rupee-dollar exchange rate, international fuel refining margins and other operating expenses also influence the final benefit to airlines.
What should investors watch?
The decline in crude oil prices could have varying implications for oil-linked companies.
While OMCs, paint manufacturers, tyre makers and aviation companies could benefit from lower input costs, upstream producers such as ONGC and Oil India could face pressure on their realisations.
